01 / Executive synthesis

What we have learned

We started by asking whether wireless channels on a 350 km/h train could be predicted. We ended with a more useful signal-processing question: can the receiver preserve reliable detection by exploiting the structure of a changing channel, even when old information becomes inaccurate?

9.08 kHz
MAXIMUM DOPPLER · 28 GHZ
For 350 km/h, not the Doppler difference between every path.
1 ms
TWO-RAY BEAT PERIOD
Result of our deliberately chosen 1,000 Hz Doppler separation.
87.6%
EXPERIMENT 4 HORIZONS
Neither single link met the chosen 5% predicted-outage constraint.
4 → 0
STALE MRC GAIN
At 0.5 ms, array power stayed 4 while a frozen combiner captured none.

Most important insight: channel strength, channel predictability, spatial direction, and decision usefulness are different quantities. A receiver may have abundant signal energy yet discard it through outdated weights; conversely, an uncertain instantaneous channel need not make every communication decision ineffective.

The notebook is a chronological consolidation of analytical results and your MATLAB outputs. It records what was demonstrated, what was assumed, and what must still be tested before any realistic railway or 6G claim.

02 / Why the research evolved

From RIS to a technology-independent question

Early work used a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) as a possible means of controlling propagation. The narrowband effective channel was written as:

heff = hd + gT Φ h,   Φ = diag(ejφ₁, …, ejφN)

But we then separated the fundamental mathematical issue from a specific hardware technology. RIS may be a future actuator, rather than the core research contribution. The larger theme became the value and useful lifetime of imperfect information in uncertain dynamical systems.

Prediction. How does Doppler estimation error affect future complex CSI?
Decision. Does prediction help choose the better link or avoid outage?
Information. When is a new pilot worth its cost, and when does old CSI stop helping?
Spatial processing. Can multiple receiving antennas retain usable energy when a scalar channel fades?
Uncertainty-aware reception. How should future receiver weights account for prediction error covariance?

The long-term application may be FRMCS and future 6G railway connectivity. The immediate contribution need not be a system specification: it can be a transparent mathematical result or a reproducible receiver algorithm.

03 / Railway wireless channel

The physical basis: Doppler, multipath, and fading

QuantityValueInterpretation
Train speed350 km/h ≈ 97.22 m/sMotion of receiver relative to propagation geometry
Carrier frequency28 GHzIllustrative mmWave carrier
Wavelength≈ 10.71 mmλ = c/fc
Maximum Doppler magnitude≈ 9.08 kHz|fD| ≤ v/λ
Distance moved in 1 ms≈ 9.72 cmAbout 9.08 wavelengths; spatial displacement alone does not determine fading
fD,ℓ = (v/λ) cos βℓ,   h(t) = ∑ℓ=1L aℓ ej(φℓ+2π fD,ℓt)

A single constant-amplitude path may rotate rapidly in complex phase without its power changing. Deep amplitude fading arises from interference between paths, not Doppler magnitude alone.

Our intentionally simple two-ray channel

hA(t) = [ej2π f₁t + ej2π f₂t]/√2
|hA(t)|² = 1 + cos(2πΔf t),   Δf = 1,000 Hz

Thus power repeats every 1 ms, with ideally complete fades at 0.5, 1.5, and 2.5 ms. This regularity comes from our chosen two Doppler frequencies, not from an inherent 1 ms railway-channel period.

Modeling boundary: actual railways include a variable number of rays, nonstationary amplitudes and angles, path delays, blockage, and sometimes waveguide effects. A realistic wideband channel is frequency selective as well as time selective.

04 / Experiments 1–2

Predictability under Doppler uncertainty

Experiment 1 — Predicting one- and two-ray channels

We used a 2 ms observation window with noisy pilots, sampled every 20 μs, and predicted as far as 10 ms into the future. Three methods were compared: hold the last observation, least-squares projection using correct supplied Dopplers, and least-squares projection using slightly incorrect Dopplers.

Channel at 10 msHold-last NMSECorrect-Doppler NMSEMismatched-Doppler NMSE
One ray2.89 dB−51.62 dB3.71 dB
Two rays4.87 dB−42.59 dB3.60 dB

The near-perfect results with supplied correct Dopplers are model-matched benchmarks, not proof that a real receiver could know those frequencies perfectly.

Experiment 2 — Predictive channel distribution

For independent Gaussian path-Doppler errors with standard deviation σf = 50 Hz, the conditional mean and variance follow from the characteristic function of a Gaussian random variable:

μh(τ) = e−½(2πσfτ)² ∑ aℓej2πf̄ℓτ
σ²h(τ) = [1 − e−(2πσfτ)²] ∑|aℓ|²

A predictive SISO linear-MMSE coefficient can use both mean and variance:

w(τ) = μh*(τ) / (|μh(τ)|² + σ²h(τ) + σ²n)

We subsequently moved beyond equalization itself toward the question of whether better information improves the action the receiver takes.

05 / Experiment 3

Useful lifetime and value of channel information

The first two-link decision experiment retained a fading two-ray Link A, but made Link B a deliberately optimistic constant-power fallback: |hB|² = 0.8. The reference SNR was 10 dB, and spectral efficiency was approximated by R = log₂(1 + γ|h|²).

RB = log₂(1 + 10 × 0.8) ≈ 3.17 bit/s/Hz
PolicyRuleWhat it tests
Stale decisionAlways choose Link A, which was strongest at t = 0Cost of keeping an old decision
PredictiveChoose link with highest conditional expected rateValue of forecasting
Risk-awareMaximize expected rate subject to predicted outage ≤ 5%Reliability–throughput tradeoff
Optional fresh pilotUse an instantaneous noisy future pilot if its benefit exceeds 5% overheadValue of measurement, idealized latency
OracleKnow the actual future channel without overheadPerfect-future-information upper bound

Why the green pilot curve can exceed the blue prediction curve

The blue policy must select a link using its existing probability distribution. A new observation allows the decision to depend on the realized measurement. The mathematical distinction is:

E[maxa Ra] ≥ maxa E[Ra]

The left side is the expected outcome of selecting with perfect future knowledge; the right side is selecting a fixed action using only prior expectations. A noisy pilot lies between these idealizations before its cost is counted.

Decision regret, not channel NMSE

Regretπ(τ) = E[max(RA,RB)] − E[Rπ]

A first-crossing lifetime can be defined as the largest continuous prefix of future horizons for which a policy's expected regret stays below the budget. That is an operational policy-performance lifetime.

Important distinction: comparing the predictive policy with fixed Link B, or calculating its regret against an oracle, does not isolate the value of old CSI. To measure that value, compare optimal decisions with and without a particular old observation, using identical background models and averaging over initial states.

06 / Experiment 4

Two uncertain multipath links

We removed the unrealistic assumption that Link B is perfectly reliable. Link A was modeled with five rays (one stronger direct contribution and four reflected contributions), and Link B with four rays. Both had path-dependent Doppler uncertainty and stochastic line-of-sight blockage. Shared speed-error and common-blockage terms introduced correlation.

hi(t) = ∑ℓ=1Li bi,ℓ(t) ai,ℓej(φi,ℓ + 2πfD,i,ℓt),   i ∈ {A,B}

The script used 1,500 Monte Carlo realizations to estimate model expectations and a separate 3,000-realization test set to evaluate policies. The model still assumed known initial path parameters and known distributions.

Information limitation versus physical limitation

Pjoint = Pr(RA < Rmin ∩ RB < Rmin)

Even perfect future CSI cannot find a feasible single link when both are simultaneously below threshold. Joint outage distinguishes failure caused by lack of knowledge from failure caused by lack of a viable path. At 10 ms the independence approximation would give 0.331 × 0.321 ≈ 10.6%, but actual joint outage must be measured from the same paired realizations because the links are correlated.

Takeaway: a better prediction cannot create received signal energy that is physically absent. This motivated moving toward spatial reception instead of studying link selection alone.

07 / SIMO Lessons 1–3

Turning a wave into a complex vector

We next replaced the single train antenna with four antennas arranged as a half-wavelength uniform linear array (ULA). At 28 GHz, d = λ/2 ≈ 5.35 mm.

a(θ) = [1, e−jψ, e−j2ψ, e−j3ψ]T,   ψ = (2πd/λ)sin θ

For θ = 30° and d = λ/2, ψ = 90°, so:

a(30°) = [1, −j, −1, j]T,   aHa = 4

Why coherent combining works

For y = ax + n, naïvely summing the four noiseless antenna signals at θ = 30° gives (1 − j − 1 + j)x = 0. Conjugate-weighted summation instead gives aHy = 4x.

x̂ = (aHy)/(aHa)

Your test recovered the QPSK symbol 0.7071 + 0.7071j exactly in the noise-free case. With independent equal-variance receiver noise, the ideal coherent gain relative to one element is 4× = 6.02 dB.

Steering-vector correlation: spatial resolution

ρ(θ₁,θ₂) = |a(θ₁)Ha(θ₂)| / (‖a(θ₁)‖ ‖a(θ₂)‖)

The correlation depends on the difference between spatial frequencies, sin θ₂ − sin θ₁, rather than on angle separation alone. Four elements can distinguish some widely separated directions exactly but poorly resolve nearby directions.

08 / Four-element array geometry

1×4 linear versus 2×2 planar

1×4 ULA: longer aperture along one axis; senses phase progression through one spatial direction cosine ux.

2×2 URA: aperture along two axes; senses both ux and uy, although with fewer elements per axis.

ux = sin θ cos φ,   uy = sin θ sin φ
aURA = [1, e−jπux, e−jπuy, e−jπ(ux+uy)]T

The planar steering vector factors into a Kronecker product of two two-element steering vectors: aURA = ay ⊗ ax with the antenna ordering used in our code.

Wave pair (θ, φ)1×4 ULA correlation2×2 URA correlationMeaning
(45°, 45°), (45°, −45°)1.000.00Planar senses the differing y-direction cosine; linear cannot
(30°, 0°), (30°, 90°)0.000.50Longer ULA aperture distinguishes these directions better

Thus a planar array is not always superior. Both contain four elements and, for the same single plane wave and noise conditions, both provide the same ideal 6.02 dB coherent array gain. Array geometry changes angular discrimination and fading statistics, not the nominal element count.

09 / Spatial matrix algebra

Gram matrices, eigenvalues, and channel covariance

For steering matrix A = [a₁, a₂], the normalized Gram matrix is G = AHA/4. With equal-length columns and complex normalized inner product c:

G = [[1, c], [c*, 1]],   eigenvalues λ± = 1 ± |c|
Angular caseULA Gram eigenvaluesURA Gram eigenvaluesRank / interpretation
Case 10, 21, 1ULA rank 1; URA has two orthogonal signatures
Case 21, 10.5, 1.5Both rank 2; URA signatures partly overlap

You verified both sets of eigenvalues in MATLAB. A small eigenvalue means the steering columns are nearly linearly dependent and inverse-based path separation becomes noise-sensitive.

From geometric Gram matrix to statistical spatial covariance

h(t) = As(t),   Rh = E[hhH] = ARsAH

If the two path coefficients are zero-mean, mutually uncorrelated, and each has variance 0.5, then Rs = 0.5 I. The four-antenna covariance eigenvalues are:

ArraySpatial covariance eigenvalues (Case 1)Trace
Linear ULA4, 0, 0, 04
Planar URA2, 2, 0, 04

The trace is the same, while power is distributed across different spatial modes. Rank and eigenvalue distribution matter for diversity and distinguishability, but do not alone establish BER or packet reliability.

Not the same matrix: AHA compares steering columns; Rh characterizes the random channel vector over an ensemble. Their nonzero eigenvalues have a relationship under specific path-covariance assumptions, but they answer different questions.

10 / Experiment 7

1×4 SIMO reception in the original two-link model

We returned to the simplest model: Link A has two rays separated by 1,000 Hz in Doppler and arriving at +30° and −30°; Link B has one ray and per-antenna reference power 0.8. Both are received by the four-element ULA.

hA(t) = [a(30°)ej2πf₁t + a(−30°)ej2πf₂t]/√2
hB(t) = √0.8 a(10°)ej2πfBt

Because the two Link A steering vectors are orthogonal, their cross-term vanishes when computing the four-antenna channel norm:

‖hA(t)‖² = (‖a₁‖² + ‖a₂‖²)/2 = 4,   for every t

At Antenna 1 alone, the gain still follows 1 + cos(2π × 1,000t), falling to zero at 0.5 ms. Spatial energy has shifted between antenna patterns rather than disappeared.

Comparing combining strategies

G(w,h) = |wHh|² / (wHw)
StrategyWeightsEffective Link A gain
Oracle / perfect CSIw(t) = h(t)4
Stale MRCw = h(0)4 cos²(π × 1,000 t)
Predictive MRCw(t) = ĥ(t)4 cos²(2π × 50 t), for deliberately opposite ±50 Hz errors
At 0.5 msApproximate gain
Link A, Antenna 10
Link A, ideal four-antenna MRC4
Link A, stale MRC0
Link A, predictive MRC3.90
Link B, ideal four-antenna MRC3.20

The companion QPSK example used independent receiver noise and ideal instantaneous channel knowledge for coherent detection. Near the first-antenna null, single-branch BER approaches 0.5, whereas four-antenna ideal MRC at 0 dB per-antenna reference SNR has theoretical BER Q(√4) ≈ 0.0228 for Gray-coded QPSK under the specified noise convention.

Physical and receiver caveats: Doppler shifts and arrival angles were prescribed independently in the ideal experiment. A railway geometry should derive both consistently from 3D propagation directions. Also, a high effective gain does not by itself guarantee correct coherent QPSK detection if residual common carrier phase is untracked.

11 / Experiment 7A

Spatial channel aging: available energy versus captured energy

Experiment 7A measured the similarity between the initial four-dimensional channel and the future channel, deliberately ignoring a common complex phase:

ρh(τ) = |h(0)Hh(τ)| / (‖h(0)‖ ‖h(τ)‖)
ηstale(τ) = ρh²(τ) = cos²(π × 1,000 τ)

The projection-matrix interpretation

Let u₀ = h(0)/‖h(0)‖. The rank-one Hermitian projector onto the original channel direction is P₀ = u₀u₀H.

Gcaptured(τ) = h(τ)HP₀h(τ) = ‖h(τ)‖² ρh²(τ)
Gmissed(τ) = h(τ)H(I − P₀)h(τ)
Gcaptured + Gmissed = ‖h(τ)‖² = 4
t = 0 ms: captured
4 / 4
t = 0.25 ms: captured
2 / 4
t = 0.5 ms: captured
0 / 4
t = 1 ms: captured
4 / 4

This is the key demonstration: strong array reception and good combiner alignment are not the same thing. A frozen set of weights may discard the entire desired signal while the total available channel energy remains constant.

Scientific qualification: the periodic recovery is a property of this deterministic, symmetric two-ray model. It does not establish that useful old CSI normally recovers periodically in real nonstationary railway channels. The reported plot did not include a printed numerical projection-identity error; that identity follows analytically and can be verified by the included script.

12 / What is established and what is not

Five enduring findings—and their limitations

Fast complex-channel variation need not imply fast power variation. A pure phase-rotating path can retain constant magnitude; two rays can create periodic interference. Analytical
Decision value is not the same as estimation accuracy. A high complex-channel NMSE can coexist with an effective robust choice. Demonstrated in toy models
Two links do not guarantee a feasible link. The chosen 5% outage requirement was violated by both modeled links at many horizons. Simulation-specific
Array geometry determines distinguishable spatial directions. Gram rank and eigenvalues follow directly from steering-vector correlation. Analytical + verified
Received energy can survive stale-combiner failure. In the orthogonal two-ray ULA, ‖h‖² remains 4 while stale combining gain reaches zero. Analytical + verified

Critical boundaries before publishing claims

Current assumptionWhy it limits interpretationPlanned correction
Two rays, fixed angles, fixed amplitudesProduces overly regular fading and ideal orthogonalityVary angles and powers; nonstationary clustered multipath
Initial path parameters knownUnderstates estimation difficultyNoisy pilots, joint parameter tracking, model mismatch
Zero-latency fresh pilotOverstates achievable information valueExplicit sampling, estimation, and action delays
Instantaneous Shannon rate as utilityNot an actual codeword-decoding or packet-delivery modelCoded BER/PER, block duration, latency constraints
Ideal instantaneous channel in MRC benchmarkOracle-style advantage may not be physically achievablePredictive/robust weights plus phase tracking
Policy regret lifetimeDoes not isolate the marginal value of old CSIBayesian with-observation vs without-observation comparison
13 / Next research steps

A disciplined path toward predictive spatial reception

The most useful next step is not a larger simulation or an immediate leap to 6G. It is to loosen one idealizing assumption at a time and see which conclusions survive.

Nonorthogonal two-ray SIMO. Change the second angle from −30° to +20°; track total array gain, channel-direction evolution, and stale/predictive combining losses. This isolates spatial correlation.
Stochastic Doppler prediction. Replace fixed ±50 Hz errors with Gaussian uncertainty. Derive and validate the predicted four-dimensional mean μ(τ) and covariance Ch(τ).
Covariance-aware combining. Compare stale MRC, predicted-mean MRC, Bayesian linear-MMSE weights, and perfect-CSI MRC with the same simulated symbols and independent evaluation samples.
Information timing. Introduce noisy pilots, overhead, processing delay, and decision-triggered measurement. Determine when new CSI improves BER or packet delivery enough to justify its cost.
Multi-link and realistic channels. Add a second uncertain SIMO link, measure joint outage, and then transition to physically consistent 3D geometry, wideband fading, MIMO, and possibly RIS.

The future four-antenna predictive receiver

yk = hkxk + nk,   μ(τ) = E[hk+τ | Dk]
Ch(τ) = E[(h−μ)(h−μ)H | Dk]
w(τ) ∝ [Ch(τ) + Rn]−1μ(τ)

Under unit-symbol-power assumptions and treating prediction error as effective interference, this covariance-aware direction maximizes a prediction-based effective SINR. If error covariance is isotropic and noise is spatially white, it reduces to the same spatial direction as predicted MRC. Any advantage must therefore come from actual covariance structure, not from relabeling a familiar receiver.

Proposed central question: Can spatially structured prediction and intelligently timed observations preserve reliable signal recovery when temporal CSI is aging—without excessive pilot overhead?

Measure what matters for the decision. Preserve what remains useful in the signal. Do not mistake a fading scalar coefficient for a loss of all spatial information.
14 / Reproducibility appendix

MATLAB reference implementations

These compact, standalone snippets reproduce essential mathematical checks from our study. The full original Monte Carlo experiments were performed separately; this appendix does not pretend to reconstruct every random trajectory from their saved plots.

Code A · Four-element steering vector and spatial phase
%% Lesson 1: Four-element ULA steering vector
clear; clc;
N = 4;
spacing = 0.5;             % d/lambda
n = (0:N-1).';
theta = 30;                 % degrees from broadside
psi = 2*pi*spacing*sind(theta);
a = exp(-1j*n*psi);
disp(a);
fprintf('a^H a = %.0f\n',real(a'*a));
figure; stem(1:N,unwrap(angle(a))*180/pi,'filled');
grid on; xlabel('Antenna'); ylabel('Unwrapped phase (deg)');
Code B · Four-element linear versus 2×2 planar array Gram eigenvalues
%% ULA vs 2x2 URA: two angular configurations
clear; clc;
d = 0.5;
posULA = d*[0 0; 1 0; 2 0; 3 0];
posUPA = d*[0 0; 1 0; 0 1; 1 1];
steer = @(p,th,ph) exp(-1j*2*pi*( ...
    p(:,1)*sind(th)*cosd(ph) + p(:,2)*sind(th)*sind(ph)));
cases = [45 45 45 -45; 30 0 30 90];
for k=1:2
 s=cases(k,:);
 AL=[steer(posULA,s(1),s(2)),steer(posULA,s(3),s(4))];
 AP=[steer(posUPA,s(1),s(2)),steer(posUPA,s(3),s(4))];
 GL=(AL'*AL)/4; GP=(AP'*AP)/4;
 fprintf('Case %d | ULA rho %.4f, URA rho %.4f\n', ...
     k,abs(GL(1,2)),abs(GP(1,2)));
 disp('ULA eigenvalues'); disp(sort(real(eig(GL))).');
 disp('URA eigenvalues'); disp(sort(real(eig(GP))).');
end
Code C · Experiment 7 + 7A: two-ray SIMO and spatial channel aging
%% Experiment 7 + 7A: four-antenna SIMO, two-ray Link A
clear; close all; clc;
c=299792458; fc=28e9; speed=350/3.6;
fDmax=speed*fc/c;
N=4; n=(0:N-1).';
steer=@(th) exp(-1j*pi*n*sind(th));
a1=steer(30); a2=steer(-30); aB=steer(10);
f1=0.9*fDmax; f2=f1-1000; fB=f1-500;
f1Pred=f1+50; f2Pred=f2-50;
timeMs=0:0.01:3; t=timeMs*1e-3;
hA=(a1*exp(1j*2*pi*f1*t) + ...
    a2*exp(1j*2*pi*f2*t))/sqrt(2);
hB=sqrt(0.8)*aB*exp(1j*2*pi*fB*t);
hPred=(a1*exp(1j*2*pi*f1Pred*t) + ...
    a2*exp(1j*2*pi*f2Pred*t))/sqrt(2);
h0=hA(:,1);
GidealA=sum(abs(hA).^2,1);
GidealB=sum(abs(hB).^2,1);
Gstale=abs(h0'*hA).^2/(h0'*h0);
Gpred=abs(sum(conj(hPred).*hA,1)).^2 ./ ...
    sum(abs(hPred).^2,1);
rho=abs(h0'*hA)./(norm(h0)*sqrt(GidealA));
eta=rho.^2;
GfromProjection=GidealA.*eta;
fprintf('Maximum projection-identity error = %.3e\n', ...
    max(abs(Gstale-GfromProjection)));
figure('Color','w');
subplot(1,2,1);
plot(timeMs,abs(hA(1,:)).^2,'b',timeMs,GidealA,'k', ...
     timeMs,GidealB,'m--','LineWidth',1.5);
grid on; xlabel('Time (ms)'); ylabel('Channel gain');
legend('A: Rx1','A: 4Rx ideal MRC','B: 4Rx ideal MRC');
subplot(1,2,2);
plot(timeMs,real(Gstale),'r--',timeMs,Gpred,'b', ...
     timeMs,GidealA,'k','LineWidth',1.5);
grid on; xlabel('CSI age (ms)'); ylabel('Effective gain');
legend('Stale MRC','Predictive MRC','Perfect MRC');
figure('Color','w');
plot(timeMs,rho,'b',timeMs,eta,'r--','LineWidth',2);
grid on; ylim([0 1.05]);
xlabel('Prediction horizon (ms)'); ylabel('Spatial alignment');
legend('Channel-direction correlation','Stale combining efficiency');
Code D · Two-path spatial covariance eigenvalues
%% Covariance from two uncorrelated, equal-power paths
% Reuse a1 and a2 from the SIMO script above.
A = [a1,a2];
Rs = 0.5*eye(2);
Rh = A*Rs*A';
disp('Eigenvalues of spatial channel covariance:');
disp(sort(real(eig(Rh)),'descend').');
fprintf('Total average array power: %.3f\n',real(trace(Rh)));
Code E · Add joint outage to the two-link Monte Carlo experiment
% Experiment 4 addition (inside the main k-loop,
% after calculating RAt and RBt on the independent test set)
jointOut(k) = mean((RAt<Rmin) & (RBt<Rmin));
% Compare this to each link's outage and selected-link outage.
% Joint outage is the ideal instantaneous selection outage floor,
% assuming successful communication if either path supports Rmin.

Recommended checks

Verify that aHa = 4; that a(+30°)Ha(−30°) ≈ 0; that ‖hA(t)‖² = 4; and that the projection identity reproduces stale-MRC gain to numerical precision. Then change only one angular parameter and compare the results.

15 / Notation and provenance

Glossary and interpretation guide

CSI
Channel state information. May refer to instantaneous channel coefficients, their estimates, or statistical information; these must not be conflated.
Doppler
Phase-rotation rate caused by motion projected onto a propagation direction.
SIMO / MRC
Single-input multiple-output reception; maximum-ratio combining weights received antenna branches to align the desired signal.
ULA / URA
Uniform linear array; uniform rectangular planar array.
Steering vector
Complex spatial phase pattern caused by a plane wave arriving from a given direction.
Gram matrix
AHA, describing overlap among columns of A.
Spatial covariance
E[(h−E[h])(h−E[h])H] for centered channel covariance, or E[hhH] as a second moment. They coincide for zero-mean channels.
Regret
Expected performance difference relative to an explicitly defined ideal comparator.
Information value
Incremental improvement in achievable decision utility given an additional observation, under matched information sets and cost accounting.

Source and evidence statement: All embedded figures were supplied as MATLAB output in the research conversation. They are simulation results. No railway field measurements, standards compliance tests, hardware measurements, or publication novelty verification are claimed in this report.

Study period: November 2026. Compiled as an independent learning and research document. Equations are analytical under the assumptions stated adjacent to them; numerical console results are transcribed from the user's MATLAB outputs. Standard 6G, FRMCS, MIMO, and RIS topics remain potential application contexts, not demonstrated deliverables.
